title: Tension-type headache
content:
Tension-type headache is one of the most common causes of head pain. It often feels like a dull, pressing, or tight band around the head, usually on both sides. It is frequently related to stress, poor posture, screen use, tiredness, or dehydration. Pain is usually mild to moderate and does not typically cause vomiting or visual changes.
Warning signs that need urgent assessment include a sudden 'worst-ever' headache, headache with fever and a stiff neck, headache with new weakness, numbness, confusion, difficulty speaking, or vision loss, or a headache after a head injury. These features are not typical of tension-type headache and require prompt medical evaluation.

title: Migraine
content:
Migraine is a common cause of moderate to severe headache, often on one side of the head, and may be throbbing. It can be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light or sound. Some people experience an 'aura' such as visual disturbances before the headache begins.
Migraine is usually not dangerous, but sudden severe headache, headache with one-sided weakness or difficulty speaking, or the worst headache of one's life should be treated as an emergency because they can indicate other serious conditions.

title: Dehydration
content:
Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid than it takes in. It can cause headache, dizziness, tiredness, a dry mouth, and dark urine. Mild dehydration can often be managed by drinking fluids gradually.
Signs of significant dehydration that need prompt medical care include not passing urine, sunken eyes, severe dizziness when standing, confusion, or being unable to keep fluids down.

title: Chest pain warning signs
content:
Chest pain has many causes, some minor (such as muscle strain or acid reflux) and some life-threatening (such as a heart attack). Chest pain that is a pressure or squeezing sensation, spreads to the arm, jaw, neck, or back, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or feeling faint can be a sign of a heart emergency.
Anyone with these features should seek emergency medical care immediately and should not wait to see if the pain passes.

title: Fever in adults
content:
Fever is a common response to infection and is often caused by viral illnesses that improve on their own. Rest and fluids are usually helpful. A fever with a cough, sore throat, or body aches is often due to a common viral infection.
Seek prompt medical care for a very high or persistent fever, a fever with a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade when pressed, difficulty breathing, confusion, or a fever that lasts several days without improvement.

title: Sore throat
content:
A sore throat is most often caused by a viral infection and usually improves within a week. Symptoms can include throat pain, mild fever, and difficulty swallowing. Warm fluids and rest can help.
Seek urgent care if there is difficulty breathing, difficulty swallowing saliva, drooling, a muffled voice, or severe one-sided throat swelling, as these can indicate a more serious infection.

title: Cough
content:
A cough is often caused by a viral respiratory infection and usually clears within a few weeks. A cough with a runny nose and mild fever commonly reflects a cold.
Seek medical care for a cough with shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing up blood, a high or persistent fever, or a cough that lasts more than three weeks.

title: Abdominal pain
content:
Abdominal pain has many causes, including indigestion, gas, constipation, and viral gastroenteritis, many of which are not serious. Mild, short-lived pain often settles on its own.
Seek prompt medical care for severe or worsening abdominal pain, pain with a high fever, persistent vomiting, blood in the stool or vomit, a rigid or very tender abdomen, or pain in a person who is pregnant.

title: Dizziness and vertigo
content:
Dizziness can mean feeling lightheaded, unsteady, or that the room is spinning (vertigo). Common causes include inner-ear problems, dehydration, low blood sugar, standing up too quickly, viral infections, or anxiety. Brief lightheadedness on standing that resolves quickly is usually not serious.
Warning signs that need urgent assessment include dizziness that starts suddenly with weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, double vision, or difficulty walking, dizziness with chest pain or palpitations, or fainting/loss of consciousness — these can indicate a stroke, heart rhythm problem, or another serious cause.

title: Shortness of breath
content:
Shortness of breath can be caused by conditions ranging from anxiety or poor fitness to asthma, chest infections, or heart or lung disease. Mild breathlessness with exertion that improves with rest is often not an emergency.
Seek emergency care for sudden or severe difficulty breathing, breathlessness at rest, blue or grey lips, chest pain, confusion, or breathlessness that comes on suddenly with one-sided leg swelling or after a long period of immobility, as these can indicate a serious lung, heart, or blood-clot emergency.

title: Nausea and vomiting
content:
Nausea and vomiting are commonly caused by viral gastroenteritis ('stomach flu'), food poisoning, motion sickness, migraine, or early pregnancy. Most cases settle within a day or two with rest and small sips of fluid.
Seek prompt medical care for vomiting that won't stop, vomit containing blood or looking like coffee grounds, signs of dehydration (very dry mouth, little or no urination, dizziness), severe abdominal pain, a bad headache with neck stiffness, or vomiting after a head injury.

title: Back pain
content:
Most back pain is caused by muscle strain from lifting, poor posture, or overuse, and improves within a few weeks with gentle activity, stretching, and over-the-counter pain relief. It rarely indicates a serious problem.
Seek urgent medical care for back pain following a significant injury, back pain with numbness or tingling in the groin or inner thighs, new difficulty controlling the bladder or bowel, new leg weakness, back pain with fever, or back pain in someone with a history of cancer, as these can indicate a serious spinal problem.

title: Fatigue and tiredness
content:
Fatigue is a very common symptom and often relates to poor sleep, stress, a recent viral illness, or overexertion. It can also be linked to conditions such as anemia (low red blood cells), an underactive thyroid, or depression. Fatigue that improves with rest and better sleep habits is usually not a sign of a serious problem.
Seek medical evaluation for fatigue that is severe, persistent for more than a couple of weeks, associated with unexplained weight loss, shortness of breath, chest pain, unusual bruising or bleeding, or fatigue that significantly limits daily activities, so an underlying cause can be checked with a simple blood test.

title: Skin rash
content:
Rashes are commonly caused by irritants, allergic reactions, eczema, or mild viral infections, and many settle on their own or with an antihistamine or moisturizer. Hives (raised, itchy welts) are usually an allergic reaction.
Seek emergency care for a rash with swelling of the lips, tongue, or face, difficulty breathing or swallowing, or a rash that spreads rapidly with dizziness (possible severe allergic reaction/anaphylaxis). Seek prompt care for a rash that doesn't fade when pressed with a glass (non-blanching), especially with fever, or a widespread painful rash with blistering.

title: Diarrhea and gastroenteritis
content:
Diarrhea is most often caused by viral or bacterial gastroenteritis and usually resolves within a few days with fluids and rest. Loose stools with mild cramping and no other symptoms are usually not serious.
Seek prompt medical care for diarrhea with high fever, blood or black/tarry stool, signs of dehydration, severe abdominal pain, diarrhea lasting more than a few days, or diarrhea in an infant, older adult, or pregnant person, as these need closer evaluation.

title: Common cold
content:
The common cold is a mild viral upper respiratory infection causing a runny or stuffy nose, sneezing, mild sore throat, and mild cough. It typically improves within seven to ten days with rest, fluids, and over-the-counter symptom relief.
Seek medical care if symptoms include a high fever, significant shortness of breath, ear pain, sinus pain with facial swelling, or symptoms that worsen after a week instead of improving, as a secondary infection may have developed.

title: Numbness and tingling
content:
Numbness or tingling (pins and needles) is often caused by sitting or lying in one position too long, mild nerve compression (such as a 'trapped' nerve), or anxiety with rapid breathing. It commonly resolves on its own once pressure on the nerve is relieved.
Seek emergency care for numbness or tingling that comes on suddenly, especially on one side of the body or face, or with weakness, difficulty speaking, vision changes, or confusion, as these can be signs of a stroke. Numbness affecting the groin/inner thighs with bladder or bowel changes also needs urgent assessment.

title: Generalized weakness
content:
Feeling generally weak or low on energy is often related to poor sleep, a recent illness, dehydration, or overexertion, and improves with rest and recovery. It can also relate to anemia or thyroid problems.
Seek emergency care for sudden weakness on one side of the body or face, weakness with slurred speech, difficulty swallowing, or confusion (possible stroke), or weakness with severe breathing difficulty or chest pain. Seek prompt care for weakness that is new, progressive, or not explained by an obvious cause.

title: Urinary tract infection (UTI)
content:
Urinary tract infections commonly cause a burning sensation when urinating, needing to urinate frequently or urgently, cloudy or strong-smelling urine, and mild lower abdominal discomfort. They are common and usually treatable.
Seek prompt medical care for fever, chills, back or flank pain, nausea/vomiting alongside urinary symptoms (which can indicate the infection has spread to the kidneys), or urinary symptoms in pregnancy, young children, or older adults, as these need timely evaluation and treatment.

title: Anxiety and panic attacks
content:
Panic attacks can cause a racing heart, chest tightness, shortness of breath, dizziness, tingling, sweating, and a sense of fear, and typically peak within about ten minutes before settling. They are common and, while distressing, are not by themselves dangerous.
Because panic attacks can feel similar to a heart or breathing emergency, chest pain, breathlessness, or fainting should still be assessed urgently, especially the first time it happens, in someone with heart disease risk factors, or if the pain spreads to the arm/jaw or comes with sweating — these features need emergency evaluation to rule out a cardiac cause.

title: Allergic reaction
content:
Mild allergic reactions can cause localized hives, itching, or a rash and usually respond well to an antihistamine and avoiding the trigger.
A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is a medical emergency: seek emergency care immediately for swelling of the lips, tongue, throat, or face, difficulty breathing or swallowing, widespread hives with dizziness or fainting, or rapid onset of symptoms after a known allergen exposure (food, insect sting, medication).

title: Muscle strain
content:
Muscle strains happen from overuse, sudden movements, or lifting, and cause localized pain, tenderness, and stiffness that usually improves within days to a couple of weeks with rest, gentle stretching, and over-the-counter pain relief.
Seek medical care if pain is severe, there is significant swelling or bruising, you cannot bear weight or use the limb, or pain does not improve after a couple of weeks, as this can indicate a more significant injury.

title: Acid reflux (GERD)
content:
Acid reflux causes a burning sensation in the chest or throat (heartburn), often after eating, lying down, or with certain foods. It is common and usually improves with dietary changes, weight management, and antacids.
Because reflux discomfort can resemble heart-related chest pain, new or severe chest pain — especially with shortness of breath, sweating, arm/jaw pain, or pain unrelated to food or position — should be treated as a possible cardiac emergency until proven otherwise.

title: Influenza (flu)
content:
Influenza typically causes a rapid onset of fever, chills, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and sore throat, and is usually more sudden and severe than a common cold. Most healthy adults recover within about a week with rest and fluids.
Seek prompt medical care for difficulty breathing, chest pain, persistent dizziness, confusion, severe or persistent vomiting, symptoms that improve then return worse, or flu symptoms in someone very young, elderly, pregnant, or with a chronic illness, as these groups are at higher risk of complications.

title: Low hemoglobin (anemia)
content:
A low hemoglobin level indicates anemia — fewer or smaller red blood cells than normal, which reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Common causes include iron deficiency (from diet or blood loss, including heavy periods), vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, or chronic disease. Typical symptoms include fatigue, pale skin, shortness of breath on exertion, and dizziness.
Seek prompt medical follow-up for a low hemoglobin result, especially with chest pain, severe shortness of breath, fainting, black/tarry stools, or heavy bleeding, as these may indicate significant blood loss or a more serious underlying cause that needs urgent evaluation.

title: Abnormal white blood cell count
content:
White blood cells (WBCs) help fight infection. A high WBC count often reflects the body responding to an infection or inflammation, and sometimes to stress or certain medications. A low WBC count can result from a viral infection, certain medications, or a bone marrow problem, and may increase infection risk.
Seek prompt medical follow-up for an abnormal WBC result, especially alongside fever, severe fatigue, easy bruising or bleeding, or recurrent infections, so the underlying cause can be identified.

title: Low platelet count (thrombocytopenia)
content:
Platelets help blood clot. A low platelet count can be caused by certain viral infections, some medications, or less commonly an immune or bone marrow condition. Mildly low counts often cause no symptoms and are found incidentally.
Seek prompt medical care for a low platelet count with easy bruising, unusual bleeding (gums, nosebleeds, blood in urine or stool), a widespread pinpoint rash, or heavy menstrual bleeding, as these need timely evaluation.

title: High blood sugar (glucose) and diabetes
content:
A fasting glucose above the typical reference range can indicate prediabetes or diabetes, especially if found on more than one occasion. Common associated symptoms include increased thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, and blurred vision, though many people have no symptoms at all.
Seek prompt medical follow-up for a high fasting glucose result. Seek emergency care for very high blood sugar with confusion, rapid breathing, severe abdominal pain, vomiting, or a fruity-smelling breath, as these can indicate a serious complication (diabetic ketoacidosis).

title: High cholesterol
content:
High total or LDL ('bad') cholesterol, or low HDL ('good') cholesterol, increases long-term risk of heart disease and stroke but usually causes no symptoms itself. It is often managed with diet, exercise, and sometimes medication.
An abnormal cholesterol result is not an emergency by itself and should be discussed with a healthcare professional at a routine follow-up. Seek emergency care instead for symptoms like chest pain, sudden weakness, or difficulty speaking, which need immediate assessment regardless of cholesterol levels.

title: Elevated creatinine and kidney function
content:
Creatinine is a waste product filtered by the kidneys; a higher-than-normal level can suggest reduced kidney function. Causes range from dehydration and certain medications to longer-term kidney disease. Many people with early kidney function changes have no symptoms.
Seek prompt medical follow-up for an elevated creatinine result. Seek urgent care for an elevated creatinine with reduced or no urine output, significant swelling of the legs/face, severe fatigue, confusion, or shortness of breath, as these can indicate more serious kidney impairment.

title: Elevated liver enzymes (ALT/AST)
content:
ALT and AST are liver enzymes; mildly elevated levels can result from fatty liver, alcohol use, certain medications, or a recent viral illness, and often improve once the cause is addressed. Many people with mild elevations have no symptoms.
Seek prompt medical follow-up for elevated liver enzymes. Seek urgent care if elevated liver enzymes come with yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), severe abdominal pain, confusion, or easy bruising/bleeding, as these can indicate more significant liver involvement.

title: Abnormal thyroid function (TSH)
content:
TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) helps regulate metabolism. A high TSH often indicates an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism), with symptoms like fatigue, weight gain, feeling cold, and constipation. A low TSH often indicates an overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism), with symptoms like weight loss, a fast heartbeat, heat intolerance, and anxiety.
An abnormal TSH is usually not an emergency and should be discussed with a healthcare professional, who may check additional thyroid hormone levels. Seek urgent care for a very fast or irregular heartbeat, chest pain, severe agitation, or confusion, which need prompt assessment.
